title: Trinity
summary: The cited passages describe the Father, Son, and Spirit in relation to one another and to God’s work. Matthew 28 names Father, Son, and Holy Spirit in the baptismal commission. John 1 speaks of the Word’s relation to God and his role in creation; John 14 records Jesus’ promise of the Advocate sent by the Father. Paul’s blessing in 2 Corinthians 13 names Jesus Christ, God, and the Holy Spirit, while Ephesians 4 speaks of one Spirit, one Lord, and one God and Father. Together these texts support a theological synthesis, though no single passage presents the whole account by itself.
historical_context: The references come from Gospel narratives and teaching, a Pauline letter’s closing blessing, and an exhortation about unity in Ephesians. The sources are the biblical texts themselves; this entry explains their wording and relationships without adding an independently sourced history of later doctrinal debates.
canonical_context: Matthew, John, 2 Corinthians, and Ephesians each speak about Father, Son, and Spirit in different contexts. Matthew’s commission names all three; John describes the Word and the Father’s sending of the Advocate; Paul’s blessing and Ephesians’ appeal to unity place the three in closely related statements. Reading them together makes the pattern visible while respecting each author’s purpose.
literary_context: The references include a commission, a Gospel prologue, farewell teaching, a closing benediction, and an appeal for unity. Their forms explain why the relationships appear differently: narrative and teaching in John, a concise triadic formula in Matthew and 2 Corinthians, and a unity confession in Ephesians. The passages are evidence for a synthesis, not interchangeable definitions.
covenantal_significance: The passages connect Father, Son, and Spirit with baptism, creation, Jesus’ mission, the church’s blessing, and communal unity. Together they show how the biblical texts associate the three with God’s work and the life of believers; the synthesis should be drawn from the group rather than attributed in full to one verse.
canonical_role: This entry gathers passages used to discuss the relation of Father, Son, and Spirit. It helps readers notice what each text says and how the passages contribute to a wider theological account, without claiming that any one text contains the entire formulation.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Trinity in its immediate context before generalizing.
Do not flatten distinct passages into one slogan; let the canon keep its own shape.
